newsitem.title: BULGARIA: POLICE AT BULGARIA PARLIAMENT FOR 7TH DAY OF DEMOS.
newsitem.headline: POLICE AT BULGARIA PARLIAMENT FOR 7TH DAY OF DEMOS.

text.p: Riot police deployed outside the Bulgarian parliament for a third day on Sunday as the opposition called fresh protests to demand an election.
After two days of clashes between police and demonstrators in which 196 people were hurt, the Holy Synod ordered masses for peace to be said in Orthodox churches around the country.
Trade unions plan strikes around the country from Monday.
On Sunday, the government responded to President Zhelyu Zhelev's refusal to let it form a new cabinet by rejecting a general election.
Taking its cue from events in neighbouring Yugoslavia, the opposition vowed daily protests until its demands were met.
Security forces wielding clubs dispersed protesters early on Saturday, ending a 10-hour siege of parliament with what a government statement described as "minimal use of force".
Opposition supporters returned hours later to their traditional rallying point outside the gold-domed Alexander Nevsky Cathedral.
Clashes erupted outside the presidency building as Zhelev, a leader of the movement that overthrew communist rule in 1989, met opposition and government leaders and security chiefs.
Ivan Kostov, leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces, urged protesters to go home and return on Sunday afternoon for a seventh consecutive day of protests.
"After the night of the long clubs, not only deputies, students and policemen are bleeding, Bulgaria is bleeding," said an editorial in Troud daily.
"The heart of the nation is bleeding which under the wise leadership of the Socialist party became poor and hungry again."
Standart blamed outgoing prime minister Zhan Videnov, who resigned on December 21 after months of criticism of his handling of the economy.

"The only ones who are profiting from the tragic events of the last few days are Zhan Videnov's circle, because the chaos and violation of parliament will cover up the incompetence and robbery of his government during the last two years," it said.
Staff of the pro-opposition Sofia municipality, helped by demonstrators, cleared debris from the riot from the square outside parliament on Saturday.
"Today we are holding a mass for those who suffered in the events of the past two days, a mass for peace," Orthodox priest Father Seraphim said at Sofia's Seven Saints church.
Asked whether the church would back the opposition as it has done in Serbia, he said: "If we take a side, this means that we reject the other and God's love is for everyone."
The Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP), largely composed of ex-communists, is half way through its parliamentary term but has lost a great deal of authority as the economy worsens.
Voters delivered a powerful no-confidence vote two months ago by electing opposition lawyer Petar Stoyanov as president with 60 percent of the vote. He will be sworn in on January 19.

"If the BSP sees this (the protests) as a state coup, the united opposition sees it as a justified wrath of people who took to the streets because they are hungry and see no future for themselves," President-elect Stoyanov told reporters after meeting European ambassadors in Sofia.
"I asked ambassadors what would the citizens of their countries do if their monthly wages were between $16 and $20 and the price of bread is $0.50," Stoyanov said.
A quarter of Bulgaria's banks are in receivership and annual inflation of 310.8 percent has slashed real incomes. The lev has fallen from 70 to the dollar a year ago to 642 now.
"These people are out on the streets not for political motives but for economic ones," Stoyanov said.

When parliament approves a new cabinet the International Monetary Fund plans to negotiate implementation of a tough fixed exchange regime as a last resort to restore confidence in the crumbling economy.
